title: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Rail | MPI, US
description: Wet fluorescent magnetic particle inspection of couplers, bolsters, side frames, axles and welds at rail shops and bridges across the US. Request a quote.
h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Railcars, Locomotives and Rail Bridges (US)
html:
Magnetic particle inspection (MPI) is the surface-crack method for the ferromagnetic steel that makes up most of a freight car, locomotive truck and railroad bridge. Atlantis NDT mobilizes qualified technicians to your shop, yard or bridge site anywhere in the United States to examine couplers, knuckles, bolsters, side frames, axles, welds and structural steel with yokes and wet fluorescent particles. For a scope and a quote, request a magnetic particle inspection quote.

Why rail equipment is a natural fit for mag particle testing

Railcars and locomotives are built from carbon and low-alloy steel that carries heavy cyclic loads: slack action in couplers, vertical and lateral loading in truck bolsters and side frames, and repeated bending in axles. Fatigue cracks start at the surface, usually at a radius, a weld toe, a casting parting line or a corner, and a crack that is open to the surface and sits in a ferromagnetic part is exactly what magnetic particle inspection reveals. The method is fast, it shows the crack's real shape and length directly on the part, and it works through thin paint and light scale when the procedure allows it.

The method has limits that matter in a rail shop. It does not find flaws buried deep in a thick casting, it cannot be used on aluminum, stainless carbody parts or brass bearings, and it needs the technician to magnetize the part in a direction that crosses the crack. Where those limits bite, ultrasonic testing or penetrant testing takes over. The rail ultrasonic page and the rail penetrant page cover those methods.

Regulations, specifications and who decides acceptance

The Federal Railroad Administration sets the safety standard through 49 CFR Part 215 for freight cars, Part 229 for locomotives, Part 231 for safety appliances, Part 238 for passenger equipment and Part 237 for bridges. Those rules define defective conditions and keep records, but they do not define a magnetic particle technique. The shop-level acceptance rules come from the AAR Manual of Standards and Recommended Practices and the interchange rules, which also govern approval of repair facilities, and from the owner's or builder's own specification.

The examination technique follows a written procedure built on ASTM E1444 for magnetic particle testing, ASTM E709 as the guide to the method and ASME Section V Article 7 where a code calls for it; our guide to Article 7 explains the requirements in plain terms. Welds on cars and locomotives are commonly examined to AWS D15.1, the railroad welding specification, and bridge welds to the welding code the owner specifies. Acceptance criteria are those in the contract documents. Our report states which table was applied and what the indication measured against it.

Our people work under the Atlantis written practice, which is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II performs the test and judges indications; an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews each report before it leaves our hands.

Components and the cracks we look for

Couplers and knuckles. Coupler bodies and knuckles are high-strength cast steel under repeated pull and buff loads. Cracks open at the pin holes, the knuckle tail and the corner where the head meets the shank, and wet-method inspection with fluorescent particles reads those areas at much finer sensitivity than dry powder. Shops often inspect couplers whenever a car comes in for repair, and many owners also set a periodic inspection requirement for knuckles.

Truck bolsters and side frames. Cast steel truck castings crack at the bolster pocket corners, the center plate bowl, the friction casting areas and where the side frame column meets the pedestal. A technician with a yoke or a coil moves around the casting, magnetizing from two directions, reading the particles under black light, and marking each indication. Rust and scale are removed at the examination areas; the procedure states how clean the surface must be.

Axles. Journals, fillets and the exposed shaft between wheel seats are examined on a stand or in a rolling fixture. Circular magnetization with a central conductor or head-shot equipment and longitudinal magnetization with a coil each find cracks in one orientation, so both are required for full coverage. A shop that magnetizes only one way finds only half the cracks, and our procedure writes both into the scan plan.

Welds and weld repairs. Underframe welds, locomotive frame welds, truck repair welds and weld build-up on worn surfaces are all examined at the toes and, where required, across the weld face. Because welds are the second most common crack site after castings, this is a standard reason to call for MPI after repair and before a car is released.

Locomotive components. Crankshaft journals, rod forgings, mounting brackets, main generator frames and truck frame welds are common targets for surface examination during a heavy repair. The procedure takes account of the part's condition: oil-soaked or carbon-laden surfaces must be cleaned to reveal indications.

Steel bridge members. Weld toes at cover plate ends, stiffener welds, hanger plates and eyebars are fatigue-sensitive details. See our job page on MPI of structural steel. Castings and forgings, including pins, are covered at MPI of castings and forgings.

Technique: equipment, field direction and particles

Most rail field work uses an AC electromagnetic yoke because it is portable and the AC field concentrates at the surface. The yoke's lifting power is verified on a test block before use, as the ASTM and ASME procedures require, and the legs are positioned so that the field runs across the expected crack. The technician then examines each area in two directions roughly at right angles. In a shop with a bench unit, head-shot and coil magnetization allow full-circumference coverage on axles and forged pins.

The wet fluorescent method is the usual choice for rail castings and axles because the sensitivity is high and the contrast under black light is easy to read. The black-light intensity at the surface is measured with a calibrated meter and held at the level the procedure sets, with ambient white light kept low enough that indications read clearly; in a bright yard a tent or darkened booth is set up. Particle concentration of the bath is checked with a settling test, and the bath is changed when it is contaminated. Where fluorescent work is impractical, such as a bridge in daylight, visible color-contrast particles on a white contrast paint are the alternative, with the lower sensitivity noted in the report.

Magnetic field adequacy is proven with a pie gauge or a shim indicator on a representative part. Technicians demagnetize parts where residual magnetism could interfere with later machining, bearing fits or welding, and they record the field residual when the owner requires it. A part made of austenitic stainless, aluminum or bronze cannot be examined by this method at all, and we say so in the quote and move to penetrant testing.

Choosing among MT, PT and UT for a rail part

Method guide for common rail components
QuestionMagnetic particleBetter alternative when it fails
Surface crack at a casting cornerPrimary methodPenetrant testing on non-magnetic or very rough surfaces
Crack under a press-fit seatCannot see itUltrasonic testing from the axle end
Subsurface casting voidPoorUltrasonic testing
Weld toe fatigue crackPrimary methodPenetrant if the steel is stainless
Section loss from corrosionNot a thickness methodUltrasonic thickness testing

Our general comparison is in the magnetic particle versus penetrant guide, and the complete guide to magnetic particle testing goes deeper on technique. The national magnetic particle testing page describes the method across other industries.

What the report contains

A rail MPI report is built so a railroad inspector or shop quality manager can check every step. Each report includes:

  • Car or locomotive number, part identity, serial or heat number and the area examined.
  • Procedure number and revision, and the acceptance table it follows.
  • Equipment: yoke or bench unit, lifting power or amperage, particle type and concentration, black-light meter reading.
  • Magnetization method and direction, and the proof of field adequacy.
  • Surface condition and cleaning method.
  • Technician name and level under the written practice, and the Level III who approved the procedure.
  • Each indication with location, length and orientation, photographed or sketched, and the accept or reject call.
  • Whether the part was demagnetized afterwards.

What to send for a quote

  1. Part list with drawing numbers and quantity (couplers, knuckles, bolsters, side frames, axles, weld repairs, structural members).
  2. Material and surface condition, including coatings or paint to remain.
  3. The specification or interchange rule you work to and its acceptance table.
  4. Where the examination will happen: bench in a shop, on the car, in a yard or on a structure.
  5. Site address, contractor orientation, badging, and track protection needs.
  6. Whether you need a black-light booth or can provide a dark area, and the shop's power supply.

Planning notes for rail facilities

Fluorescent inspection needs darkness, so we plan around indoor bays or portable tents, and we check power and lighting at the site. Cars with fresh paint may need the coating removed locally. Yard examinations depend on weather; wet surfaces and rain interfere with dry-powder work and with bath concentration, so the plan names a weather fallback. Roadway worker protection and the railroad's own safety rules apply on or near live track. Our technicians complete the contractor safety orientation the facility requires before work starts.

We do not perform radiography in the United States, we do not run in-track rail flaw detection, and the engineer or railroad inspector, not Atlantis, decides when a car or structure returns to service.

Where we work in the United States for rail

  • Chicago: the country's densest rail interchange, with heavy yard and repair activity.
  • Kansas City: a gateway where several railroads meet, with intermodal and car repair work.
  • Omaha: main-line corridor and large shops on the Plains.
  • Fort Worth: yards, locomotive servicing and car repair in North Texas.
  • Louisville: Ohio River rail bridges and busy classification yards.
  • Birmingham: steel, coal and a long history of freight car work in the Southeast.
  • St. Louis: large river crossings and extensive interchange.
  • Atlanta: Southern rail hub for intermodal and general freight.

Training your own mag particle inspectors

If you would rather qualify your own staff, we run SNT-TC-1A-based MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, with hands-on practice in the magnetic particle simulator. The employer certifies its own people under SNT-TC-1A, so we can also help you write the program through written practice development.

faq.q: Which rail parts can be inspected with magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Any ferromagnetic steel part: couplers, knuckles, bolsters, side frames, axles, welds, locomotive forgings and structural steel on bridges. Aluminum, stainless carbody parts and brass cannot be examined this way and go to penetrant testing instead.

faq.q: Is wet fluorescent MPI better than dry powder on rail castings?
faq.a: For fine fatigue cracks at casting corners and axle fillets, wet fluorescent is more sensitive and easier to read under black light. Dry powder is quicker on rough or hot surfaces, but we state the sensitivity difference in the report.

faq.q: Does magnetic particle inspection find cracks under a wheel seat?
faq.a: No. It shows only cracks open to the surface or very close to it, so it cannot see cracks buried under a press fit. Ultrasonic testing from the axle end covers that area, and many owners combine the two methods.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects an indication on a coupler or bolster?
faq.a: The acceptance table in your contract, the AAR requirement or the owner's repair specification decides, not Atlantis. We record location, length and orientation and compare each indication to that table so your inspector can confirm.

faq.q: Do you demagnetize axles and pins after the test?
faq.a: Yes where the procedure or your standard requires it. Residual magnetism can affect machining, bearing fits and later welding, so the report states whether the part was demagnetized and, when you ask, the measured residual field.

faq.q: Can you test painted freight cars without stripping them?
faq.a: Thin, well-bonded paint is often acceptable if the procedure allows it and the field adequacy is proven on a representative part. Heavy or flaking coatings are removed at the examination areas, and the quote says which applies.

faq.q: Can MPI inspect railroad bridge welds and pins?
faq.a: Yes for ferromagnetic steel, using yokes, and either wet or visible dry particles depending on light and weather. Traffic protection and access come from the owner and railroad, and the owner's engineer decides what the findings mean for the structure.

faq.q: Can you shoot radiographs of rail castings and welds?
faq.a: No. Industrial radiography in the United States is licensed under NRC and Agreement State rules, and Atlantis does not perform it. Where your code allows, ultrasonic testing can be the volumetric method for castings and welds.

faq.q: What do you need to quote a rail MPI job?
faq.a: A part list with drawing numbers and quantity, the material and coatings, the specification and acceptance table, whether the work happens in a shop or in the field, and the site address with any orientation and track protection requirements.
